'''Caroline Elinor Hussey''' (3 December 1941 – 11 May 2017) was an Irish [[microbiologist]] and academic. She served as president of the [[Irish Federation of University Teachers]] (IFUT) from 1989 to 1992.<ref>{{cite web|title=Death of Dr Caroline Hussey|url=http://www.ifut.ie/content/death-dr-caroline-hussey|website=Irish Federation of University Teachers|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref> In 1994 she sat on the Expert Group investigating the circumstances of the 1977 contamination with Hepatitis C of the [[BTSB anti-D scandal|Blood Transfusion Service Board's Anti-D]] product. 
In the same year she was appointed the first female registrar and deputy president of [[University College Dublin]] (UCD) and remained in that post until her retirement in 2004.<ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/education/tributes-paid-to-former-ucd-registrar-caroline-hussey-on-her-death-1.3082489 | title=Tributes paid to former UCD registrar Caroline Hussey on her death | date=13 May 2017 | newspaper=The Irish Times|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref> She was Chairperson of the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment from 1995 to 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ncca.ie/en/About_Us/NCCA_20_years_a_growing.pdf|title=NCCA: 20 years a-growing|website=NCCA website|access-date=7 July 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171116071817/http://ncca.ie/en/About_Us/NCCA_20_years_a_growing.pdf|archive-date=16 November 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Birth and education ==
Caroline Hussey was born on 3 December 1941 to Frank and Aileen Hussey. Frank Hussey was lecturer and housemaster at [[Albert College (Dublin)|Albert College]], the [[University College Dublin|UCD]] agricultural school in Glasnevin (now [[Dublin City University|DCU]]), and the family lived on campus for a time. She completed her primary and secondary education at the St. Mary's Holy Faith Convent in [[Glasnevin]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/people/consummate-scientist-and-mathematician-with-well-honed-political-instincts-1.3138919|title=Consummate scientist and mathematician with well-honed political instincts|date=1 July 2017|newspaper=The Irish Times|access-date=7 July 2017}}</ref>

Graduating from UCD in 1962 with a degree in Biochemistry, Hussey went on to complete a PhD at [[Trinity College, Dublin|Trinity College Dublin]] in 1966. She continued her research at TCD and was awarded a postdoctoral fellowship at [[Harvard University]]. In 1973 she returned to UCD, where she was appointed as lecturer in [[industrial microbiology]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ucd.ie/t4cms/Dr%20Caroline%20Hussey%20CSHW%20Obituary.pdf|title=Dr Caroline Hussey Obituary}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web | url=http://www.ucd.ie/newsandopinion/news/2017/may/18/drcarolineelinorregistrarucd1994-2004/ |title=Dr. Caroline Elinor Hussey: 1941 – 2017 | date=18 May 2017 | website=University College Dublin}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
During her time as lecturer in industrial microbiology, Hussey served as a member of the Governing Body of UCD and was also a member of the Senate of the [[National University of Ireland]] (NUI).<ref name=":1" />

She had a particular interest in the area of health and safety. This interest led to the initiation of a Diploma in Health and Safety, a multidisciplinary programme that was taught in a number of Irish Universities. Ultimately, this contributed to the passage of the first Health, Safety and Welfare at Work Act in Ireland, in 1989.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

=== Senior academic administration ===
In 1994, Hussey was appointed Registrar and Deputy President of UCD, a position she held until her retirement in 2004<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.ucd.ie/news/oct04/chussey.htm | title=University College Dublin | website=ucd.ie | access-date=14 July 2017}}</ref> She was known for her rigorous defense of academic standards and addressing quality of teaching at UCD.<ref name=":1" /> In 1996, she became chair woman of the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment making her, according to a profile in the ''[[Irish Times]]'', "arguably the second most influential woman in Irish education".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/education/ireland-s-second-mistress-1.22364|title=Ireland's second mistress|date=16 January 1996|newspaper=The Irish Times|access-date=15 July 2017}}</ref> [[Niamh Bhreathnach]] was the Minister for Education at the time, and Caroline Hussey strongly supported her decision to abolish third level fees.

==Political activism==
Having joined the Labour Party in the 1970s, when the late Frank Cluskey was in the ascendant, she became the first female director of elections in the country, performing this role for Ruairí Quinn through the 1970s and 1980s, a decade of political turbulence with five general elections, two of which were in 1982.

==Public Service==
Together with her  UCD colleagues, Peter Start and deputy-president Tom Walsh, she established the National Centre for Safety and Health in Ireland and contributed to the first Health, Safety and Welfare at Work Act 1989, under the auspices of her friend and political comrade, the then Minister for Labour, [[Ruairí Quinn]] which established the [[Health and Safety Authority]].

In March 1994, Minister for Health, [[Brendan Howlin]] T.D. appointed Dr. Hussey along with [[Miriam Hederman O'Brien|Dr. Miriam Hederman O'Brien]] and Dr. Alistair Bellingham to the Expert Group investigating the circumstances of the 1977 contamination with Hepatitis C of the [[BTSB anti-D scandal|Blood Transfusion Service Board's Anti-D]] product administered in maternity hospitals.
On January 27, 1995, the Expert Group delivered their report<ref name="ExpertGroup">{{cite web | title=Report of the Expert Group on the Blood Transfusion Service Board / Ireland Department of Health | url=https://www.lenus.ie/bitstream/handle/10147/46041/10489.pdf |access-date=11 March 2022 | work=Lenus |date=20 January 1995 |language=en}}</ref> to the new Minister for Health, [[Michael Noonan (Fine Gael politician) | Michael Noonan]] T.D. who subsequently had it published.

In 2011, Hussey was appointed by the Minister for Education [[Ruairi Quinn]] as part of an advisory group to convene the forum on Patronage and Pluralism in the Irish primary education sector.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.education.ie/en/Press-Events/Press-Releases/2011-Press-Releases/PR11-3-28.html|title=Minister Quinn announces the establishment of a Forum on Patronage and Pluralism in the Primary Sector | date=28 March 2011 |website=Department of Education and Skills|access-date=15 July 2017}}</ref> The group published their report the following year.<ref>{{Cite book | title=The Forum on Patronage and Pluralism in the Primary Sector : report of the forum's advisory group | last1=Coolahan | first1=John | last2=Hussey | first2=Caroline | last3=Kilfeather |first3=Fionnuala |publisher=Department of Education and Skills | year=2012 | location=Dublin}}</ref>

== Crime Fiction ==
Under the pseudonym H.J. Forrest, Hussey published two crime novels; ''Publish or Perish'' (1991)<ref>{{Cite book|title=Publish or Perish|url=https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3783175W/Publish_or_perish|last=Forrest|first=H.J.|publisher=Glendale Press|location=Sandycove, Co. Dublin |year=1991|isbn=978-0907606925}}</ref> and ''Murder by the Book'' (1992).<ref>{{Cite book|title=Murder by the book|last=Forrest|first=H. J.|date=1992|publisher=Gill and Macmillan|isbn=9780717119752|location=Dublin|oclc=29185350}}</ref>
Both novels were set in the familiar surrounds of UCD and South Dublin suburbs, which gave rise to great speculation in academic circles as to the author's true identity.<ref name=":0" /> The mystery was eventually solved by Dr Tony Scott, Dean of the Science Faculty who unmasked Dr. Hussey.

== Later life and death ==
Although she retired from academia in 2004, Dr. Hussey kept in touch with the UCD Centre for Safety and Health and never missed
their annual Breakfast Seminars. 
Having been vice-president of UCD football club for more than 20 years, she continued to be a regular at UCD soccer matches and other events, such as the UCD Strictly Come Dancing event.<ref name=ucdobit>{{Cite web| title=Dr Caroline Hussey CSHW Obituary| url=https://www.ucd.ie/t4cms/Dr%20Caroline%20Hussey%20CSHW%20Obituary.pdf |website=University College Dublin | date=15 May 2017 |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref> 

She died in [[Dublin]] on 11 May 2017 after a short illness.<ref name=":0" />
